title: Heidi Klum Dressed Up as a Severed Human Hand for Her Annual Halloween Party
description:
Is it really Halloween without Heidi Klum?

	The supermodel, who has become known for her over-the-top costumes, has returned for another year of h
body:
Is it really Halloween without Heidi Klum?

	The supermodel, who has become known for her over-the-top costumes, has returned for another year of her annual Halloween party, this time opting to dress as a realistic-looking severed human hand.

	At last year’s party, Klum dressed as the mythological monster Medusa, which featured a headpiece decorated with writhing snakes and a trailing tail, while her husband, Tom Kaulitz, went as an ancient Greek soldier she had turned to stone. It ultimately took a team of 15 artists to create her costume, Klum told Variety at the 2025 event.
	

	“There still needs to be people that create moments with real people … to me, it’s like a beautiful art,” she said. When asked about her elaborate look, she shared, “This is only good for the night. Tonight. Everything goes down the drain, so to speak, in the shower.”

	This year’s celebration marked the 25th year of Klum’s Halloween party. Some of her past looks include notable characters such as E.T., Fiona from “Shrek,” Jessica Rabbit and the werewolf from Michael Jackson’s “Thriller,” as well as creatures like a peacock, worm and butterfly.

	Earlier this year, Klum hosted the 22nd season of “Project Runway,” where she also served as a judge alongside Nina Garcia and Law Roach. Klum returned to the fashion competition series last year after previously exiting in 2018. Prior to her departure, she hosted the show for 16 seasons since its 2004 debut on Bravo.

	Alongside Tim Gunn, Klum created a new fashion competition show titled “Making the Cut” for Prime Video in 2020, which ran for three seasons.

schema.headline: Heidi Klum Dressed Up as a Severed Human Hand for Her Annual Halloween Party

title: ‘Green Room’ Director Remembers Patrick Stewart as a ‘F—ing Sweetheart’ and Credits Him for Rescuing the Film: He ‘Swooped Down’ ‘Into Our Cruddy Ass Movie and Saved Us’
description: “Green Room” writer and director Jeremy Saulnier paid tribute to late actor Patrick Stewart, who starred in the film and whom he credits with savin
body:
“Green Room” writer and director Jeremy Saulnier paid tribute to late actor Patrick Stewart, who starred in the film and whom he credits with saving the day when they were “close to shutting down,” during a 10th-anniversary screening of the 2015 film in Los Angeles on Friday. Stewart died one day earlier, on Thursday, at 86.

	“Who’s sad as fuck we lost Patrick Stewart yesterday? Me,” said Saulnier during his introduction to the movie. “I came here to shamelessly promote Slayground, but instead, I’m just gonna celebrate Patrick Stewart. He had no business doing this movie. He had plenty of opportunities otherwise.” His star power revitalized the production when it was “at the point of no return,” said Saulnier, and no one had been cast as Darcy Banker, the skinhead leader Stewart ultimately played. “We’re fucked, and we were close to shutting down,” he said.
	

	Then, “Patrick Stewart, out of the blue, sort of expressed interest in the project,” said Saulnier. “And in a whirlwind about a week later, I was on the phone with him. I left the stage, ‘Maybe we’re gonna have to break down the sets and shut the whole movie down.’

	He continued: “Instead, this dude came out of nowhere, from way above our sort of zone, and just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us, and said yes. And the movie was instantly greenlit; we moved forward. And I thank him for just taking that leap and making ‘Green Room’ a thing.”

	Saulnier remembered the actor as a “fucking sweetheart, true gentleman, a kind leader to our whole cast,” and recounted his idea to add “a little something” to one scene: “I was like, ‘What is it, Patrick?’ He’s like, ‘Well, during this one part of the scene, when the camera’s coming through there, I’d like to say, “Fuck!” And I was like, ‘And?’ ‘Just fuck.’ Permission granted, sir,” Saulnier recounted. “And I just knew that he was completely aligned with the film, its aesthetic, its intentions and with me as a filmmaker, and it was just this lovely, lovely thing.”
	

	Stewart died after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia, according to a statement on his Instagram account. He was best known for his roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and as Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films, among many other film and TV credits.

Jeremy Saulnier took a break from editing ‘SLAYGROUND’ to introduce a 10th anniversary screening of ‘GREEN ROOM’ at Alamo Drafthouse in LA and pay tribute to Patrick Stewart.Saulnier revealed that Stewart saved ‘GREEN ROOM’ from being shut down and personally requested to add… pic.twitter.com/GCBgsHo9OU— Film Updates (@FilmUpdates) October 31, 2026

title: Judge Dismisses Trump’s Wall Street Journal Defamation Lawsuit Over Published Epstein ‘Birthday Book’ for a Second Time
description: A federal judge has once again dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation claims against the Wall Street Journal over a 2025 report by the paper
body:
A federal judge has once again dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation claims against the Wall Street Journal over a 2025 report by the paper that a 2003 birthday letter to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein was purportedly written by Trump.

	Trump’s lawsuit “falls short of pleading actual malice,” wrote U.S. District Judge Darrin P. Gayles in his opinion on Saturday. “Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.” Judge Gayles dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot refile the claim.
	

	In April, Judge Gayles ruled that the lawsuit “fails to adequately allege actual malice,” a legal standard in the U.S. for proving defamation. At the time, the court dismissed the complaint “without prejudice,” since he had only made one attempt to state his claims.

	Trump sought at least $20 billion in damages on two counts of defamation in the initial suit, filed in July 2025. He sued the WSJ, its parent companies Dow Jones & Co. and News Corp, the reporters on the story and Rupert Murdoch.

	“We have just filed a POWERHOUSE Lawsuit against everyone involved in publishing the false, malicious, defamatory, FAKE NEWS ‘article’ in the useless ‘rag’ that is, The Wall Street Journal,” Trump wrote at the time on Truth Social. “I hope Rupert and his ‘friends’ are looking forward to the many hours of depositions and testimonies they will have to provide in this case.”

title: Pandemic-Era Longing to Gather Fed Qiu Jiongjiong’s Tokyo Competition Title ‘Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting’
description:
Chinese painter and filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong began shaping his new film during the pandemic. 

	With the world suddenly forced to pause, he tells V
body:
Chinese painter and filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong began shaping his new film during the pandemic. 

	With the world suddenly forced to pause, he tells Variety, people felt an urgent desire to return to everyday life and to gather around a table.

	That idea became the starting point for “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting,” which is competing at the Tokyo International Film Festival. The film connects four eras through food and shared meals, with each chapter approaching the pleasure of eating, and its meaning, through its own fantastical vocabulary. An opening title card presents “Fuxi” as a phrase that evokes both the delight of food and the act of eating.
	

	“This may be the film with the most dialogue I’ve ever had, but I couldn’t understand a word of it,” says Taiwanese star Lee Kang-sheng, the longtime lead of director Tsai Ming-liang’s films. He plays two elderly women from different eras, including a dying grandmother in the film’s prehistoric chapter. The entire film is spoken in the Leshan dialect of Sichuan province.

	Lee Kang-sheng worked with several dialect coaches, Qiu says. “I was drawn to the mysterious quality about him, which felt perfectly suited to a character from ancient times,” he says. “That gave me the idea of asking him to play a woman.”

	Taiwanese actor Lee Hong-chi, who also worked with dialect coaches, plays Song dynasty poet Su Dongpo. He had long admired Qiu’s visual work. “I only found out I was playing Su Dongpo when I got the script,” he says. “The dialect was a challenge for me, too, but I really wanted to be part of the film because of its nonrealistic aesthetic and the world Qiu had created.”
	

	Unlike Qiu’s previous feature, “A New Old Play,” which focused on an individual’s personal history, “Fuxi” unfolds in sequence across four eras through four short stories. Qiu says he used the meals at the center of each chapter to approach questions of life and death.

	“Through the individual lives of the characters, I wanted to explore a kind of relativity specific to this film – the relationship between the large and the small, or between a meal and the sun and the moon,” he says.

	“Fuxi” was Qiu’s first time working with professional actors, an experience he says has broadened his creative ambitions. His solo exhibition, “Qiu Jiongjiong: Fuxi: A Feast for the Universe,” runs at Chengdu’s A4 Art Museum through Jan. 31. Built around three Sichuan-style banquets, the show uses painting, video and installation to explore the region’s culture and its ideas about life and death. Qiu is still developing his next project and has yet to settle on its subject or medium.

	Asked about a recent film that made an impression on him, Qiu singles out Christopher Nolan’s epic “The Odyssey,” saying he is fascinated by its reconstruction of history and its aesthetic. Lee Kang-sheng says he recently watched Stanley Kubrick’s “2001: A Space Odyssey” for the first time after Tsai and his actor friend Chang Chen recommended it.

	“I was surprised that such a brilliant film could have been made so long ago,” he says. “It also made me more curious about different kinds of films.”

	Lee Kang-sheng, whose work in Tsai’s “Walker” series has drawn international attention, has just wrapped filming on Argentine director Iván Fund’s science-fiction film “Bodies of Summer.” Asked what he might like to try after taking on dialect-heavy dialogue and female roles, he says he usually lets roles find him.

	“Whether I’m playing a gangster or an old woman, I want to bring my own version of Lee Kang-sheng to the role,” he says. He adds that whenever one of Jason Statham’s films comes on television, he still wants to stop and watch it to the end. An action or martial-arts film, he suggests, could give him a chance to step outside his familiar screen image.

schema.headline: Pandemic-Era Longing to Gather Fed Qiu Jiongjiong’s Tokyo Competition Title ‘Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting’

title: Paul Bettany Says He ‘Blew Out’ 10 Blood Vessels in His Eye While Filming ‘VisionQuest’: ‘I Was Just Wildly Overacting’
description: Paul Bettany might play Marvel superhero Vision, but an on-screen acting choice while filming “VisionQuest” nearly cost him that very sense when th
body:
Paul Bettany might play Marvel superhero Vision, but an on-screen acting choice while filming “VisionQuest” nearly cost him that very sense when the “Iron Man” actor accidentally popped 10 blood vessels in his eyes.

	“I was pretending to have a device on my head that is doing something to my brain, and I was just wildly overacting, and I blew out about 10 blood vessels in my eye,” said Bettany during a recent appearance on “Jimmy Kimmel Live.” “It was a lesson in less is more,” he laughed, before Kimmel showed audiences a shot of his blood-filled eyeball.
	

	Bettany continued, explaining that his eye stayed that way for two weeks and production had to “take it out” of the final shots. “The irony is the actor playing Vision is kind of myopic, you know,” said Bettany. “Can’t see a thing when I take my glasses off, which is great, depending on the actor,” he joked.

	“VisionQuest,” Marvel’s long-awaited eight-episode spinoff of “WandaVision,” debuted on Disney+ on October 14. Bettany stars as the android and former Avenger, and the TV series marks his return to the MCU after having roles in “Avengers: Age of Ultron,” “Captain America: Civil War,” “Avengers: Infinity War” and “WandaVision.” Within the universe, he was first introduced in the first “Iron Man” movie as J.A.R.V.I.S., the AI voice that controls Tony Stark’s powerful suit of armor.

	The show also stars James Spader, who reprises his role as Ultron from “Avengers: Age of Ultron,” Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, James D’Arcy, Orla Brady, Emily Hampshire and Ruaridh Mollica.

schema.headline: Paul Bettany Says He ‘Blew Out’ 10 Blood Vessels in His Eye While Filming ‘VisionQuest’: ‘I Was Just Wildly Overacting’

title: Frank Miller on Why He’s Relieved There Are Fewer Comic Book Adaptations Now: They Were ‘Really in Danger of Losing Their Souls’
description: Comic book writer and screenwriter Frank Miller – whose work includes “300,” “Sin City” and “Batman: The Dark Knight Returns” – returned this week
body:
Comic book writer and screenwriter Frank Miller – whose work includes “300,” “Sin City” and “Batman: The Dark Knight Returns” – returned this week to Lucca Comics and Games, an event that spans the gamut of geek culture and pop entertainment.

	As well as speaking at the event, to coincide with the 40th anniversary of “Batman: The Dark Knight Returns,” Miller also introduced “Frank Miller – American Genius,” Silenn Thomas’ documentary about his impact on popular culture.
	

	Variety spoke to Miller about politics, art and why he’s relieved there are fewer comic book movies this year.

	Would you agree that there has been a slight dip in the comic book to movie pipeline?I would hope so. Yeah, really. It had really gotten so out of control that comics had started losing much of their own identity. I have been arguing vehemently for comics to start asserting their own purpose again and asserting their own identity as a literary form.

	Do you think there were too many comic book artists and writers aiming for movie and TV deals?Oh, without question. Just because the appeal of not just the money, but the fame, respect and glory of working in the most powerful medium in history is undeniable, but I think that it was a little too heady a wine, in that comics were really in danger of losing their souls in the process.

	It very much seemed to be superhero movies in particular.Oh, that was all it was. It was partly because the technology caught up with us. So the one thing comics could do that nobody else could do was the ridiculous pyrotechnics and everything, right? But if you think of it, the die was cast back in the 1970s with the movie slogan “You’ll believe a man can fly” where they actually made Superman’s flight convincing, and now they can do, you know, virtually anything that can be imagined.
	

	Some of your finest work has been inspired by cinema, but has not necessarily involved superheroes: “Sin City” and “300” for instance.Well, yes, my entire oeuvre has been dedicated to defining and redefining the hero, and sometimes making him as ugly as possible, as in Marv and “Sin City,” and other times torturing the hero: as with Hartigan in the “Sin City: That Yellow Bastard” story. The exploration of the hero is just infinitely fascinating. Once you let go of the idea of the hero being society’s voice, it becomes more an examination of the human spirit.

	As well as the heroes, you create astonishing, extreme worlds. But it seems that we live in a world which is almost impossible to exaggerate.I often have remarked that doing the next “Martha Washington” would be difficult because the first one happened. And my parody of Ronald Reagan is now in the White House, right? But there’s always somewhere else to go. Now you would parody what my country has turned into, and what the world has turned into, it’s fascinating dark material, indeed.

	It’s almost like Dante looking at hell and going, “I see some verses here.”There’s no shortage of inspiration now. This is indeed a supercharged time, because in the course of the 20th century, there were two gigantic realignments, through the two world wars, particularly World War II, which was a gigantic, unifying event. World War II was the advent of American hegemony, but now we’re at the other side of the American hegemony. America has become much like Rome: spread so far and so rich and powerful that it has lost its center. It is no longer Thomas Jefferson’s country, for instance. It is no longer the land of the free and the home of the brave. It’s become quite a bloated thing, and of course this is exactly when we start waving the flag more than ever, right?

	When I see the MAGA signs I ask whether by saying “again,” you are saying that it’s not great. There are so many contradictions within all of that, but this is a global situation. The old order is, as Bob Dylan put it, rapidly aging, and so everywhere you look, there’s an empire crumbling. Look at the thrashing old Soviet Union, right? And what it’s dissolving into, when a tiny brave country is bringing it to its knees. China has become a paranoid concentration camp. So we’re definitely seeing a change in the matrix. Speaking of the Chinese, this does bring to mind the old curse: May you live in interesting times. We live in interesting times, don’t we?
	

	Watching the documentary “American Genius” I noticed you didn’t seem to listen to music when you work.I’ll either work and just have the street sounds, or I’ll have NPR on, listening to world news. That’s helpful to me, especially when I’m drawing. It helps me remove one sphere of my mind from play to a certain extent, and to let the verbal side of my mind be occupied, and let the freer, more relaxed, visually-oriented side take over because most of the drawing work is the actual clinical, decisive part of the illustration. I work that out on a sheet of tracing paper, and then when it comes to executing the drawing, I want to be as relaxed as possible and not be consciously thinking too much, revealing more. So if I’m drawing someone who’s angry, for instance, I’m striking the face with brush strokes that are angry ones. It gets into a more jazz rhythm. Whereas when I’m plotting a story or when I’m writing dialog that is verbal work. So I want to be focusing more on that side of my mind.

	What next?Well, I’m working with the great Italian artist Milo Manara, who is renowned for his erotic and often funny comic book work. He asked me on stage once if I would write a “Sin City” story for him. He’s the only artist I could ever imagine doing one with, because I’ve always drawn them all myself. But this is the one exception I’ll make because … I told him on stage, being glib: Yes, I’ll do it but he’d have to learn how to draw women.

	[Miller also announced during his stay at Lucca that he would be collaborating once more with Japanese artist Peach Momoko with whom he’d previously worked on “Tears of the Spider Queen” for Marvel.]

schema.headline: Frank Miller on Why He’s Relieved There Are Fewer Comic Book Adaptations Now: They Were ‘Really in Danger of Losing Their Souls’

title: Tokyo Asian Future Drama ‘Jani Be Good’ Probes Silence and Motherhood in a Chinese-Indonesian Family, Marking Ariani Darmawan’s Return
description: Indonesian filmmaker Ariani Darmawan stepped away from directing for years to raise a family. Her first feature, “Jani Be Good,” which is playing i
body:
Indonesian filmmaker Ariani Darmawan stepped away from directing for years to raise a family. Her first feature, “Jani Be Good,” which is playing in the Tokyo International Film Festival’s Asian Future competition, turns that experience into a portrait of four women across three generations.

	“I stopped making films for over 10 years because I was having a kid and looking after my family, so getting back to it was all I really wanted,” Darmawan tells Variety.
	

	Unfolding across four December days in the lead-up to Christmas, the film follows 13-year-old Jani after she overhears a fight between her 18-year-old sister Julia and their mother Winnie, and Julia leaves home. Winnie, a single mother who works as an accountant and fills fruit hamper orders on the side, grows short-tempered with the daughter who stayed. Jani, who has been secretly trading messages with Julia, leans on her grandmother, Oma, who makes spring rolls to sell so she can put money aside for her own cremation. The household is Chinese-Catholic.

	The four leads are Chempa Puteri, Sigi Wimala, Tutie Kirana and Hyori Mika. Darmawan co-wrote the screenplay with Cyntha Hariadi. Taurisia produced for Palari Films, the Jakarta-based company she runs with fellow producer Muhammad Zaidy. Palari, founded in 2016, opens the film in Indonesian cinemas on Dec. 10.

	Taurisia, an old friend, called Darmawan in 2022 with an offer to direct a family drama, a genre the filmmaker says she loves. As a working mother, she adds, family life is what she most wants to talk about right now, and only recently has she noticed how much unseen care work it demands every day. Becoming a mother, Darmawan says, also changed the way she sees her own.
	

	“As a kid, I watched her keep the family running, rummaging through things at her desk, making phone calls, cooking dinner, but I never wondered how she felt,” she says. “It took having my own family, in my late thirties, to understand how exhausting and all-consuming it is.”

	As the youngest in her own family, Darmawan grew up being treated as the one who understood least. “But that’s exactly what gave me the freedom to watch things from a distance,” she says. “You could say you can only see the constellation when you’re standing outside it.”

	Jani is constantly told to be good, though she already is. The film stays with her as she slowly starts to see her mother, sister and grandmother as people with wants and failings of their own. Darmawan says people tend to assume that a household made up entirely of women will find a way to get along.

	“Family problems are the same whether it’s all women or a mix of men and women, if there’s a problem in there to begin with,” she says. “Communication can break down between women too, especially because of the power dynamics in a family, where the mother, especially if she’s the breadwinner, feels she has the most right to speak the loudest.”

	In many Asian families, she says, disagreements are met with silence to avoid hurting a relative. “But that ends up hurting us even more,” Darmawan says. “If it keeps getting held in and never confronted, it stays a wound and gets passed down to the next generation.”

	She sees the same pattern in many all-female households, where staying quiet to avoid making a scene becomes a way of getting through the day. The film never says so outright, she adds, but it shows in how the women protect themselves at home, behind a gate that stays shut and windows fitted with bars.

	Winnie responds to Julia’s departure by working harder, and her care reaches her daughters as a stream of instructions and corrections. “I didn’t want Winnie to be a villain, because she isn’t one,” Darmawan says. “I think I understand Winnie because I’m a mother too. I know how easy it is to feel like the one who has the right to speak the loudest. So I didn’t want to judge her.”

	From the start, Darmawan, Hariadi and Taurisia agreed that no character would carry the blame, drawing on their own families and their experiences as daughters and mothers. The bigger creative hurdle, Darmawan says, was the co-writing itself. She had mostly written her own films before, and this time had to turn Hariadi’s prose into scenes that would hold an audience without losing the writer’s voice.
	

	Her earlier work ran from shorts to documentaries. Her short “Sugiharti Halim” competed at Clermont-Ferrand and screened at Rotterdam and Busan, while “Silenced” also played Rotterdam. She describes those projects as small-scale, homebound and DIY, a training ground for watching quietly and letting people and spaces carry a scene.

	Taurisia says she has followed Darmawan’s shorts since the early 2000s and always expected her to come back to filmmaking. What sold Palari on the project was the maturity of Darmawan’s take on womanhood and motherhood.

	The production was compact. The team shot in 13 days, a first for Palari, in a house in Bandung. Darmawan, Hariadi and the four lead actors first read the script together in that house two months before cameras rolled, rehearsed in Jakarta, then returned to the location for the final two weeks of prep with cinematographer Teoh Gay Hian and production designer Suherina. None of the four actors knew each other beforehand, so the casting process included chemistry tests built around Puteri.

	“I sat in on the whole process, but when it comes to the final call, I like to leave it to the director,” Taurisia says. “She’s the chef, and she knows her ingredients best.”

	Palari won Locarno’s top award, the Golden Leopard, at the festival’s 74th edition with “Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash” (Seperti Dendam, Rindu Harus Dibayar Tuntas). Its output since 2017 has ranged from “Posesif” and “Aruna and Her Palate” to Netflix original “Borderless Fog” (Kabut Berduri), “Dear David” and this year’s “Sleep No More.” For “Jani Be Good,” the company applied for international development funding without success. At home, Taurisia says, festival success brings diversity, recognition and a stronger portfolio.

	“On the other hand, it can make our films look ‘too artistic’ or ‘not accessible enough,’ and local investors may see the project as risky,” she says.

	The producer points to distribution as the bigger structural problem: Indonesia has exhibitors, but no distributors that reach across the archipelago. One of filmmakers’ biggest nightmares, she says, is having a film judged over a single Thursday-to-Sunday stretch before cinemas decide whether to keep it. To counter that, Palari launched Kelas Komunitas Palari (Palari Community Class) this year, a workshop series teaching film communities around the country to stage screenings and paid watch parties in their own regions. “Jani Be Good” is the program’s first test.
	

	“Many directors struggle to make a second film after their first, and this gap in the film value chain doesn’t help,” Taurisia says. “How can we build film careers, let alone sustainable ones?”

	Palari’s slate mixes returning and first-time directors. Edwin is attached to coming-of-age film “Menari dengan Bayangan” (Dancing With My Shadows, working title), a collaboration with Hindia, the solo project of singer-songwriter Baskara Putra. Aditya Ahmad’s first feature “Goldfish” picked up three awards at the Busan Asian Project Market, and Khozy Rizal’s debut feature, “I Wanna Dance With Myself,” is also on the slate.

	Darmawan, who founded the independent library and bookstore Kineruku, intends to keep directing, though she expects further films to come about organically around her family and the bookshop. “As for themes, I’m open to anything, as long as it has sad and sweet relationships between people,” she says. “That’s where things get complicated and interesting.”

schema.headline: Tokyo Asian Future Drama ‘Jani Be Good’ Probes Silence and Motherhood in a Chinese-Indonesian Family, Marking Ariani Darmawan’s Return

title: Taika Waititi Slams ‘Klara and the Sun’ Critics as ‘Irrelevant,’ ‘Sad Lost Souls’ and Says He Hasn’t ‘Read a Review’ in 15 Years: ‘But I Do Listen to the People’
description: Taika Waititi has taken to social media to defend “Klara and the Sun,” his latest directorial effort, amid poor reviews and bleak box office number
body:
Taika Waititi has taken to social media to defend “Klara and the Sun,” his latest directorial effort, amid poor reviews and bleak box office numbers, sharing an Instagram post featuring the film’s poster and its Rotten Tomatoes audience score of 78%. (In contrast, the critic score is 28% — the “Jojo Rabbit” director’s lowest yet).

	“I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people,” Waititi wrote in his caption. “So this Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus became critics. The same people who also hated Jojo Rabbit. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”
	

	When it debuted in theaters last weekend, “Klara and the Sun” landed at a staggering No. 15 with just $720,000 from 880 locations, and Sony scaled back its theatrical footprint after reviews panned the movie as a “calamitous” and “strained, whimsical comedy that’s ruinous.”

	Jenna Ortega, who stars as the film’s titular android, also recently revealed in a Vogue interview that she doesn’t read reviews of her films because “that would send me into a psychosis of some sort” or check the box office updates when her team sends them her way because “I don’t want it to become a numbers thing.”

	Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel, “Klara and the Sun” takes place in a dystopian future as an obsolete companion android (Ortega) tries to bond with her new owner, a young sick girl named Josie.

	See Waititi’s post here.

schema.headline: Taika Waititi Slams ‘Klara and the Sun’ Critics as ‘Irrelevant,’ ‘Sad Lost Souls’ and Says He Hasn’t ‘Read a Review’ in 15 Years: ‘But I Do Listen to the People’

title: ‘Before the Rain’ Director Milcho Manchevski on Tokyo Competition Title ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover,’ Whistleblowing and the ‘Death of Beauty’ in Cinema
description: Milcho Manchevski, the North Macedonian director whose 1994 debut “Before the Rain” won Venice’s Golden Lion and earned an Oscar nomination, is bac
body:
Milcho Manchevski, the North Macedonian director whose 1994 debut “Before the Rain” won Venice’s Golden Lion and earned an Oscar nomination, is back in competition at the Tokyo International Film Festival with “Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” a project stalled for years after he accused his country’s film agency of corruption.

	The dark comedy centers on Malina and Viktor, a sister and brother getting by on the fringes of post-Communist Macedonia by pilfering busts of national heroes cast in bronze, along with manhole covers, and selling off the metal. When a job goes wrong and Viktor is seriously hurt, Malina cuts a deal with a crooked doctor. The siblings end up on the run, and eventually take shelter with the doctor’s wealthy mother, Todora, who is blind.
	

	“I wanted to tell a story about a kind of love that is rarely at the center of films, yet it is so beautiful: the love between a brother and a sister,” Manchevski tells Variety. “It can be fierce, complicated, sometimes painful, but also unconditional like no other type of love.”

	The director also took inspiration from traditional Macedonian songs about sisterly love, which he calls poignant and at times shocking. Of Malina and Viktor, he says: “They are far from ideal people. But they are deserving of understanding and affection. I am interested in people as they are, with their contradictions, not as examples of how people should behave. Idealized characters make for bad movies.”

	The siblings break the law and sometimes make terrible mistakes, but Manchevski says he had no wish to turn them into objects of pity. He sees the pair’s refusal to think of themselves as victims as a way of reclaiming their own story.
	

	“Poverty is not picturesque. It is painful and dehumanizing,” he says. “We should be careful not to romanticize it, or to pretend that people can simply overcome it through courage and good intentions. The circumstances that shape these lives are real, and they are political.”

	For Manchevski, the busts stand for the values a society claims to honor while it abandons people like Malina and Viktor. “They would rather eat than venerate the past and the ideals,” he says. The manhole covers are a plainer matter: everyday infrastructure that turns into a hazard the moment it disappears. Still, he adds, the covers “keep a lid on the ugliness of society, on its septic underground” until someone pries them loose.

	Manchevski says he follows the characters and story rather than picking a genre in advance. “People can be in terrible circumstances and still be funny. They can be cruel and generous, ridiculous and moving,” he says. “Life does not keep these things separate, so I don’t see why a film should.”

	Having grown up under Communism, he is wary of films that advertise their moral correctness and offer little beyond it. “Art should not talk down to its audience,” he says. “It should open up a world, not close the discussion.” He also mourns what he calls “the death of beauty in cinema today,” though he hopes the tide will turn.

	The film unfolds in two movements. The first trails the siblings through a rough and unpredictable world; the second tightens its focus on their inner lives. “Sticking to genre rules is a bit like painting by numbers – it makes the film easier to make and easier to digest, but it seldom results in profound work,” Manchevski says.

	This marks Manchevski’s fourth time at the Tokyo festival; his previous feature, “Kaymak,” played in competition in 2022. “I love Tokyo,” he says. His other credits include “Dust,” which opened Venice in 2001, “Shadows,” “Mothers” and “Willow,” as well as an episode of HBO’s “The Wire.”

	“‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’ was blocked for years after it was financed. After I reported corruption at the Film Agency that goes all the way up to the Prime Minister, I faced political harassment, a media smear campaign and criminal proceedings,” Manchevski says.
	

	Manchevski reported the alleged corruption in 2020 and 2022, and the project had first been approved in 2023. He says he won two court cases against the agency and that institutions including the State Commission for Prevention of Corruption and the State Audit Office confirmed his account. The Venice Film Festival, Whistleblowing International and Transparency International lent him their support.

	“I would not reduce the situation of all Macedonian filmmakers to my own experience,” he says. “But when a filmmaker can be prevented from working for political reasons, that points to a dysfunctional society.”

	Once the blockade lifted, Manchevski shot the feature alongside “Good People,” a documentary about those affected by the Kočani nightclub fire.

	The film comes from a specific place, but Manchevski says the problems it explores are not confined to North Macedonia. “It is not only a third world problem. We are all the third world today,” he says. “In that sense, wealth inequality is the new global warming.”

	The film is a co-production spanning North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Serbia, Albania, Italy and the U.K. Manchevski values the exchange of perspectives such partnerships bring, provided there is trust and a shared commitment to the work. “Many festivals and (European) film funds have abdicated their role in promoting and boosting brave films,” he says. “This ecosystem is complicit in the death of beauty in contemporary cinema.”

	The cast includes Sara Klimoska, Filip Trajkovikj, Sonja Mihajlova, Dejan Lilich and Petar Mirchevski. Stefano Falivene served as cinematographer and David Munns as production designer.

	Jane Kortoshev produced the film, with Banana Film as the lead production company. Gala Film (Bulgaria), Sense Production (Serbia), Tirana Film Institute (Albania), Berkeley Media Group (U.K.) and Amarcord Production co-produced, in association with Italy’s Augustus Color. Galina Toneva, Milan Stojanovic, Agron Domi, Yu-Fai Suen, Ludovico Cantisani d’Auria and Augusto Pelliccia are co-producers, while Manchevski, Kiril Kirilov, Svetlana Levicheva and Tatiana Forese serve as executive producers. Steven Barnes is the U.K. associate producer. Coccinelle Film handles world sales.

	Next up for Manchevski is “Homecoming,” which he describes as a simple story about regret and forgiveness. “I am elated that I finally cracked it open by reducing it to its emotional and narrative essence,” he says.

schema.headline: ‘Before the Rain’ Director Milcho Manchevski on Tokyo Competition Title ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover,’ Whistleblowing and the ‘Death of Beauty’ in Cinema

title: Phoebe Bridgers Makes L.A.’s Intuit Dome Into an Intimate Space Full of Love, Grief, Light Shows, ‘Peter Pan’ Cosplay and a Great Billie Eilish Duet: Concert Review
description: So, in talking about the marvel that was Phoebe Bridgers‘ opening night at L.A.’s Intuit Dome Friday night, which part of the show do you talk abo
body:
So, in talking about the marvel that was Phoebe Bridgers‘ opening night at L.A.’s Intuit Dome Friday night, which part of the show do you talk about first? Would it the emotionally riveting middle section of the show, in which Bridgers used the no-phones setting to elaborately explore, in song and in monologue, her complicated family dynamics, including figuring out how to grieve the death of a sometimes abusive father who had both a positive and impact on her life? You don’t get moments of candor and quiet devastation like that in an arena show every day, or decade.

	Or, would it be the part later where Billie Eilish came out in her pink onesie pajamas? The duet on “Savior Complex” where she and Eilish on the stage danced around in their Peter Pan-inspired costumes? Because, come on. Dude.



	

					Phoebe Bridgers and Billie Eilish embrace at Intuit Dome in Inglewood, Calif., Oct. 30, 2026
									Matt Grubb
	



	This “Lost Weekend Tour” stop at the Intuit Dome (the first of three sold-out weekend shows there wrapping up her U.S. tour) provided a wealth of moments of moods to talk and write about, so no one can be blamed for picking either the most moving or goofiest bit of the show to single out. The Eilish cameo will surely outweigh all other highlights in the popular vote that is (for once, picture-less) social media. For the audience in the house down in Inglewood, anyway, it was a magnificently holistic experience, putting the lie to the idea that a Bridgers concert is finally going to be anything but a joyfully celebratory experience, these days. Even if she is also perfectly equipped to answer Leonard Cohen’s final rhetorical question: You want it darker? 

	Possibly the most talked-about aspect of this tour has also been the most seemingly irrelevant: the artist’s insistence that all smart devices be locked up in Yonder pouches, which is not completely uncommon for shows in smaller theaters where the artists want to keep a secret, but has rarely been done at the arena level. (It’s probably no small expense on the tour budget, when you’ve got 18,000 pouches and the employees to manage them as a line item… so there’s some sacrifice involved for Bridgers as well as the audience.) Having turned in my Apple Watch as well as phone, I kept having the same thought rolling around in my head during Alex G’s opening set, as well as the intermission: I know the end. But I don’t know the time.

	But probably few on hand would argue that it didn’t make for a more mesmerizing experience, the sensation of being alone in the dark with no more illumination than what was coming off the stage and the audio verification that everyone in the same oversized space is also feeling the feels. I hate to go overboard in congratulating a crowd, but there was a specifically impressive moment during the starkest number of the night, “Still Standing,” which Bridgers performs just accompanying herself on acoustic guitar, sans band. There was a pin-drop silence throughout this performance, but toward the end of the song, Bridgers’ strumming got so hushed that I feared unnecessary applause would break out because part of the crowd might assume it was ending, as often happens in concerts. But this audience was too savvy to be faked out, and their silence was upheld during that most delicate of passages — which, combined with the lack of the visual intrusion of an 18,000-strong filming crew, made for some heart-ripping magic.



	

					Phoebe Bridgers at Intuit Dome in Inglewood, Calif., October 30, 2026
									Wes Eillis
	



	Bridgers did comment on her choice to be a bit of a pioneer in banning phones at this big a level. She framed it not in the language of being a techno-scold but in wanting to allow for the ability to speak freely without self-consciousness about how it would look the next day to a world that cares a lot less than those that managed to score a ticket. In the middle of the part of the show where she spoke about her mom and dad, she said, “I can’t thank you enough for being willing to be without your devices for a couple of hours,” noting that otherwise the revealing things she’d just said “would have been a TikTok moment, where someone who doesn’t like my face would have been commenting on it.”

	At the same time, she had a sense of humor about it, a little later on, when, right after Eilish left the stage in her costumed PJs, Bridgers blurted, “You don’t have your phones. Ha ha!” If it seemed like a gloat for a second, the crowd seemed willing to laugh with her. Prior to Eilish’s guest spot, they’d also gotten a value-added moment when Muna came out to join Bridgers for “Silk Chiffon,” another moment that made everyone grab for their absent phone, like it was a phantom limb. Everyone enjoyed getting these viral moments as a tradeoff in not actually being able to take them viral.


	Bridgers performed 14 out of 16 tracks from her two-and-a-half-month-old “Lost Weekend” album (leaving out only a couple of short interludes), and her faith that her audience would want to hear this latest release thoroughly dominate the setlist was not misplaced. The album veers back and forth — sometimes within the same song — between her mixed feelings about her father and his death, on the down side, and on the up side, her apparently contented relationship with Bo Burnham. It departs from these two threads occasionally, as with “The Governor’s Waltz,” a breakup song about a past relationship of some note that is poignant in its sense of disappointment but also hilariously snarky in spots. But mainly it traverses between the poles of, on one hand, grappling with death and its aftermath, and on the other hand, a big old fresh romance. The concert, like the album, feels like a successful case of holding two thoughts at the same time — the irreversibility of death and grief and the major head rush of true love. You could spend the rest of your life writing about these two subjects, so it’s no wonder that “Lost Weekend” feels like such a full meal, and certainly a big journey to take an audience on for an hour and 55 minutes in concert.


	Bridgers reserved most of her most intimate material for a second act in which she moved to a B-stage toward the back of the floor section. There, she sat down on the floor, cross-legged, in front of a synthesizer, which was initially malfunctioning. “Oh no, it’s broken,” she said. “Of course this happens at home.” Although she might not have been in the mood for irony right at that moment, it did seem a little bit appropriate that the song she was about to do, the title track of “Lost Weekend,” was a song about a broken engagement. Once the synth’s powers were restored, she was able to make her way through the spooky ballad, which came to a partial line a lot of people might relate to after an intense relationship has gone awry: “You know me, and I’ll never forgive you for that.” On record, the song then goes into a minute-long instrumental coda that is a bit unsettling. Live, it was something else altogether — a complete aural and visual freakout in which shards of light hit all parts of the audience in fast and intense bursts as the sound system went into overload. The lobbies of the Intuit included the usual warnings about strobe being part of the production, but they really weren’t kidding in this instance.
	



	

					Phoebe Bridgers with Muna at Intuit Dome in Inglewood, Calif., October 30, 2026
									Wes Ellis
	



	But that last minute of “Lost Weekend” (the song) was the only part of the night anyone could call assaultive. The crucial middle section of the show continued to deal with tough emotions, but in a gentle fashion. To the B-stage she brought out four acoustic players — handling fiddle, mandolin, upright bass and banjo/mandocello — to back her up on what felt like an extended spacy-hootenanny section. Her previous album’s “Graceland Too,” about a friend in need, was a gorgeous standout here. And it was followed by its cousin from the new album, “Haunted,” which on record represents a Boygenius-meets-Nickel Creek moment (literally and figuratively) — the Americana song of the year, maybe? — and which sounded just as beautifully sprightly with this lineup. Ironically, it’s a song about the old feeling of dreading touring that is so joyful in its rootsy execution, it convinces you that Bridgers has changed her mind and loves being on the road now.

	And then shit got personal. “I’ve always loved Halloween; it’s always been my favorite,” she said, explaining why everyone in her band and crew was dressed up as someone from “Peter Pan,” from the Darling family to pirates to a crocodile… with Bridgers herself as Pan, the original lost boy. Looking to her offstage brother for confirmation of the memory, she said, “I was supposed to be Tinkerbell when I was little,” but she “thew a tantrum” and insisted on being Captain Hook — “internalizing some of my feelings about men,” she supposed.
	

	That led to the more pertinent musings that set up the harrowing songs that followed. “My dad died about four years ago — complicated guy, to say the least,” she said. Anyone who’d heard her sing about their sometimes estranged relationship on her biggest hit, “Kyoto,” already knew that, but there was much farther to dig now. She said that they had “a relationship where we’d talk about every two years,” usually at a point that she’d be working on material for her next project, and indicated that she has struggled with going through several of those cycles now — writing, recording, album release — in his absence, yet talking more than ever about him in song.

	“Shout out to my mom,” Bridgers added, thanking her for “giving me space to grieve someone who was abusive… and made himself into such a main character in my life, when all my mom ever did was help me. Go, Mom. Anyway, this one is for my dad,” she added, as the preface thst led into “Still Standing,” the song she sang by herself on acoustic guitar, with simple, spirit-rending lines like: “Feeling indifferent, wearing black / Sometimes I want you back / But not today.” 

	That was followed by what might be the most powerful song from the new album, the majestically portentous “As Above,” which references her father’s abusive moments before going into a moving bridge about the possibilities of the present day. “You won’t have to believe in magic,” she wailed at someone — presumably her current love; “Leave it to me and I’ll make it happen,” she vowed. As the music crested (provided by her band warming back up over on the A-stage), Bridgers stood facing a thin sheet of white light, filled up with what looked like a shower of celestial glitter. As a conjuring of what the rejuvenating power of love might look and sound like amid a life of casual disappointments, this conjoining of songcraft and stagecraft was good enough to send a chill down your spine, in you believe in all that stuff, and in how a really great concert might manifest it.
	

	And, then, yeah, it was a short trip from that heavy catharsis to the sight of Bridgers and Muna lead singer Katie Gavin indulging in a Peter Pan-vs.-Captain Hook swordfight during “Silk Chiffon.” But of course, it was the more upbeat pleasures and spirited anthems of the show’s first and third acts that set the sparer drama of the second act in stark relief. Certainly there were some weighty songs as well when Bridgers was with her full band on the main stage, but these came with the promise of a healthy scream — like the extended howl that inevitably erupts amid the audience as well as on-stage as the climax of “I Know the End” — instead of the anticipation of a pin-drop.

	The production design is worthy of a few sentences of praise. There’s a bit of UFOlogy that lingers in some of Bridgers’ visuals, but it’s mostly not too obvious. The show begins with Bridgers and her band on the A-stage under a half-dome that could be a giant igloo. It tilts up to reveal not just the musical ensemble but an additional circular screen, onto which can be projected, for example, a moonscape (during, duh, “Moon Song”). A giant curtain behind the stage — which I was never quite sure if it was a real curtain or an LED representation of one — is a backdrop onto which are projected the requisite big-screen images of Bridgers and her band, for the folks not in front. The practically infinite ripples in this curtain ensure that the video of the musicians being thrust onto it remains a little bit distorted and not too digitally literal, while satisfying the need in the rafters to see the star as something more than a distant avatar. (Needless to say, maybe, Bridgers is cool enough that this is one of the few arena productions out there that doesn’t have pyro or confetti cannons.)

	What’s most remarkable about the Lost Weekend Tour is its ability to be two things at once, or in close juxtaposition. It’s a conflicted elegy, and a romantic comedy. It’s a big, boomy soundscape, and also a celebration of folk music, in its most delectably finger-picking moments. It’s a showy, expensive-looking extravaganza that never seems the slightest bit too small for its 18,000 seats, but it also has the intimacy of a soul-baring bullshit session back at the apartment after a night out at the club. And it brings us Phoebe Bridgers, who can be pretty hardboiled, in her lyrics, but who will always carry a vocal or personal softness  wholly uncharacteristic of just about anyone else at this level of pop stardom.
	

	That sort of spectacular intimacy is kind of a miracle, in other words. So it’s all right if you don’t have your phone, because you were never going to capture all that on it anyway.

	Setlist for Phoebe Bridgers at Intuit Dome, Inglewood, Calif., Oct. 30, 2026:

	A-stage:The OutsideMotion SicknessKill MeThe Governor’s WaltzLost BoysDVD MenuGarden SongMoon SongLiberty TreePanorama (instrumental)

	B-stage:Lost WeekendFuneralGraceland TooHauntedStill StandingAs Above
	

	A-stage:BobbySilk Chiffon (with Muna)Waiting RoomSavior Complex (with Billie Eilish)I Can’t WaitKyotoI Know the End

	Encore (Bridgers on B-stage, band on A-stage):Lost Weekend (Reprise)Scott StreetNever Going Back! (without Bridgers)

schema.headline: Phoebe Bridgers Makes L.A.’s Intuit Dome Into an Intimate Space Full of Love, Grief, Light Shows, ‘Peter Pan’ Cosplay and a Great Billie Eilish Duet: Concert Review

                            5:24 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Lynn Krieger -- the wife of the legendary guitarist of The Doors, Robby Krieger -- is dead ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... Lynn died in her sleep Thursday after battling a longtime illness.
      
    
            We're told paramedics were called to Robby and Lynn's Beverly Hills home just before noon for a possible cardiac arrest, but Lynn was already dead when fire and police personnel arrived.
      
    
            Law enforcement also received a call for a natural death. Her official cause of death is not known at this time.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Lynn met Robby and the rest of The Doors at a New York City nightclub in 1967. They married in 1972 and had one child together -- a son named Waylon.
      
    
            She was 79.

title: Johnny Lopez, Beloved Former TMZ Writer, Dead at 55
description:
Johnny Lopez
                          Beloved Former TMZ Writer Dead at 55
body:
Johnny Lopez
                          Beloved Former TMZ Writer Dead at 55
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Johnny Lopez, one of the brilliant writers who helped launch TMZ.com and shape the irreverent, hilarious voice that became synonymous with the site, has died.
      
    
            Johnny was there in TMZ's early days and was instrumental in developing the unique tone that set the site apart.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            He was a beloved member of the TMZ family, someone whose personality was every bit as memorable as the stories he wrote.
      

            Johnny created many of the franchises on the site that we still use today... such as 'Memba Them?, 'Who'd You Rather', 'Good Genes, Good Docs?' and 'We're Just Sayin'.'
      
    
            Johnny also worked for Access Hollywood, Queerty, People, Outsports and Dish Nation. He was also a passionate advocate for LGBTQ rights ... and a die-hard Madonna fan.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The Men's Health Foundation was a cause close to Johnny’s heart. Those wishing to honor his memory can make a donation to the organization here.
      
    
            He will be deeply missed.
      
    
            Johnny was 55.
      
    
            RIP
